source.title: Ultrafast artificial intelligence: machine learning with atomic-scale quantum systems
source.authors: T. Pfeifer; M. Wollenhaupt; M. Lein

record.tranche_reason: The study reports training and held-out classification results for a quantum model atom, a new kind of system and task setting for the broad generalization claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports success rates on natural handwritten digits for its model atom, but does not test fitting arbitrary or random labels, standard gradient training, or any of V1–V8's specified conditions or measurements. Its results concern a distinct physical learning system and do not establish the versions as stated.
record.test_reason: The study measures held-out digit classification by a simulated, evolutionarily optimized quantum atom. It tests none of V1–V8: it reports no random-label memorization, width sweep, architecture or optimizer comparison, batch-size intervention, dropout intervention, sharpness correlation, or memorized-example removal.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors present a proof-of-principle simulation of optically programmed atomic digit classification and interpret improved success on unseen images as generalization. They propose future experimental implementations and larger quantum systems.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a simulated 20-level quantum atom, shaped laser fields and an evolutionary optimization procedure rather than standard gradient training of neural networks.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports three model variants with different coupling strengths or state energies; their individual plotted values are not stated numerically. It says the basic optimization scheme may be limited by computational resources in a high-dimensional search space.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report that training and unseen-test classification success increase together across three example optimization runs of a simulated 20-level atom; routine training and test success are above 40% and approximately 30%, respectively.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An evolutionarily optimized laser-programmed model atom can improve classification of unseen handwritten digits after training on natural digit examples.

record.problems: Proof-of-principle simulation with only 100 training and 100 test examples; no uncertainty estimates or control comparisons are stated. The optimization is evolutionary rather than gradient-based, and the reported result does not test arbitrary-label memorization.

untested.parts: Coexistence of near-perfect random-label fitting and natural-label generalization under the same architecture and training recipe; chance-level held-out accuracy with random labels.
Test error as network width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under limited or broader tuning and recovery interventions.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that reduce the penalty.
Effects of adding or removing dropout and weight decay across data and augmentation regimes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness ranking generalization gaps and comparison with norm- or margin-based measures.
Test-accuracy effects of removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Generic held-out improvement does not establish any specified claim version. Figure 4 itself is unavailable in the supplied text, so variant-specific numerical values cannot be verified. The paper cites Exploring Generalization in Deep Learning as background but does not test its sharpness findings.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and chance-level test accuracy; the specified architectures, datasets and training recipes.
Width sweep past interpolation and test error as a function of width.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparisons and tuning conditions.
Large versus small batch training and recipe adaptations.
Dropout and weight-decay interventions and their effects.
Sharpness or other measured properties correlated with train–test gaps.
Removal of memorized examples and resulting test-accuracy change.

rows.subject: 20-level model atom
rows.operation_detail: Evolutionary optimization of program fields for handwritten-digit classification.
rows.value: Routinely, success rates of > 40% and ∼ 30% are achieved for training and test sets, respectively.
rows.note: The paired percentages are aggregate success rates for this variant; they are not reported as arbitrary-label capacity or as a test-error comparison under standard gradient training.
rows.check: The >40% training and approximately 30% test success rates summarize routine performance in the Figure 4 caption; they are not explicitly specific to the state-independent-coupling variant. Training and test accuracy should be separate measure rows. Neither measure establishes any listed version.
